title: Federal court blocks Illinois assisted suicide law for religious objectors during lawsuit
text:
Federal court blocks Illinois assisted suicide law for religious objectors during lawsuit
LAX Leader
Some Catholic hospitals and other religious objectors in Illinois will not be required to promote the state's assisted suicide policy while a federal lawsuit challenging the mandate proceeds. Springfield Bishop Thomas Paprocki, a Lutheran care home, and several Christian doctors filed the suit in U.S. district court earlier in August, arguing that the Illinois “End-of-Life Options” law compels doctors to participate in assisted suicide against their conscientious objections.
On Aug. 21, the district court issued an order restraining enforcement of these rules against the plaintiffs while litigation continues. The Thomas More Society, representing the plaintiffs, announced this order on Aug. 24.
Peter Breen, head of litigation at the Catholic legal group, said in a press release that the order is “a critical first victory” for religious objectors involved in the case.
Dr. Mary Keen Kirchoff, one of the doctors participating in the suit, said in a press release that this means she can focus on caring for her patients without worrying about jeopardizing her career by adhering to her faith: “I am grateful I can keep practicing medicine according to my integrity and my faith without that threat hanging over me,” though she acknowledged this arrangement is only “for now.”
The district court clarified that its block applies only to those named as plaintiffs; otherwise, Illinois may continue enforcing its assisted suicide law statewide. Governor JB Pritzker signed this measure into law in December 2025. The legislation allows physicians to assist “qualified terminally ill patients” with ending their lives using prescribed lethal medication if two physicians determine they have less than six months to live and possess sufficient mental capacity.
Pritzker said when signing it into law that it "honors [the] strength and courage" of residents facing terminal illness. A similar temporary block was agreed upon by New York state officials after a coalition of religious sisters challenged New York's own assisted suicide statute; as with Illinois, relief there applies only to those involved while litigation is ongoing.
